One line of thought considers what each headline could open up, such as a follow-up on who bears the cost of a low price. Another compares the language with similar published pieces and asks whether the wording matches what the draft can show. Possibilities and concrete examples illustrate different sources of information on the S/N axis. Either colleague can consider both.

Considering only new angles may leave the meeting without a decision. Relying only on past coverage may leave a worthwhile idea unexplored. The team can choose a headline the draft supports today and record which assumptions it would need to check for a follow-up.

In a fictional family group chat, an aunt forwards an image making an alarming claim about a common food. Two relatives see the same image and neither has read the original source.

One question is whether the source can be traced: who published it, when, and whether the image quotes it accurately. Another is what the original evidence would need to show for the claim to follow. Both relatives can ask both questions and may reach the same judgment.

A practical reply might ask for the original link and say what the screenshot leaves unclear. A private note may feel easier if the sender would take a public reply personally. Either type can use either channel. The point is to distinguish what is known from what was only forwarded.

This example is about evaluating and discussing a claim. It reaches no conclusion about the food or what someone should eat.
